question_text: Please identify an issue currently in the mainstream media and explain how this is likely to impact the clients that HFW represents and the type of work that the firm undertakes (350 words)
sample_answer: One issue that has and will continue to impact HFW and its clients is the rising tensions between China and Taiwan. It is thought that China's current military assertiveness around Taiwan may eventually become a full-scale invasion at some point over the coming months. Pertinent to HFW's shipping sector of expertise, events in the region have led major shipping groups to seek to incorporate break clauses into existing contracts with Chinese shipbuilders. These clauses would, in theory, allow western businesses to walk away from deals if western governments were to impose sanctions on China. Sanctions imposed on Russia as a result of its invasion of Ukraine were extensive and sudden, so businesses are expressing an eagerness to ensure they hedge themselves against trade regulation risk if similar measures are imposed by western governments on China. However, industry experts have emphasised the difficulty of this process. Many of China's shipbuilding companies are state-owned including China State Shipbuilding Corporation; one of the largest and most influential in the world. This makes the process of incorporating clauses that allow companies to walk away from deals nearly impossible as the government simply won't agree, especially given that many businesses are already contracted into long-term deals. In light of the issues facing shipping companies in relation to China, I believe it represents an exciting opportunity for HFW to meet the demand for advice in this area. Following the broad interpretation of sanctions clauses in Lamesa Investments Limited v Cynergy Bank Limited, the firm can assist clients by incorporating sanctions clauses into contracts which will enable them to operate in line with domestic law without breaching contractual terms. Although it may be difficult to implement clauses that allow companies to rescind contracts, there is also a scope for HFW, through its trade sanctions expertise and market-leading shipping practice, to negotiate alternative solutions for clients. This could include incorporating contractual provisions that allow for compensation in the event of domestic sanctions, for example. Clients seeking sanctions clauses will require a focus on careful and precise drafting which HFW is undoubtedly well-equipped to offer.

question_text: Please use this section to tell us about yourself, your skills, achievements and why you want to train as a solicitor and work at Ashurst. (738 words)
sample_answer: I want to work as a commercial lawyer as it is engaging to immerse myself in the commercial aspects of a client's business. For example, as a debt recovery paralegal, I acted on behalf of several 'Big Six' energy providers. I was exposed to the commercial implications of the recent energy crisis and the breakdown in trust between our clients and their customers. I helped to rebuild this relationship by creating a complaints log to refer specific issues, such as Ombudsman complaints, to the client. I also ensured that any complex details were explained clearly to debtors, such as Ofgem guidelines throughout the Supplier of Last Resort process. As a result, our Q2 recoveries exceeded targets by over 150% and we received minimal complaints from debtors. I enjoy considering both commercial and legal issues in conjunction; it highlights the real-world impact that the law can have on businesses. As such, I would embrace the opportunity to work at Ashurst, where lawyers act as commercial, rather than purely legal, advisors. I am applying to Ashurst specifically as the firm has a friendly and collaborative culture. Whilst all firms state they have a friendly culture, during the Evening with Ashurst Event, I learned that these were principles genuinely embedded throughout the firm. For example, trainee Saba Nasrolahi shared how after just two weeks at the firm, she was involved in high-level social inclusion and mobility meetings. The fact that a trainee can participate in prominent internal discussions highlights that Ashurst is a firm that is accepting of trainees and places value on their input. Personally, I enjoy applying myself within a collaborative and accepting culture. As a team leader at the [redacted university] Students' Union, I was given agency to create new initiatives. I organised a [redacted event] charity event, involving over 25 staff members and raising over £1,000 for Sport In Mind. As someone who thrives in a friendly working culture, I see myself as a natural fit for a career at Ashurst. Throughout university, I worked as bar staff for my Students' Union. Approaching my role with enthusiasm, I made a significant impact and I was promoted to Team Leader within just two months. As Team Leader, I developed communication, delegation and leadership skills. In freshers week - the busiest time of the year - I managed a different team every night, composed mostly of new staff. To tackle the problems this posed, I formally introduced myself to each team member and explained their role for the night. Additionally, I ensured that experienced staff were spread throughout the venue so that inexperienced staff could learn by osmosis. This approach allowed us to achieve great results. One memorable night included leading the team to a record-breaking revenue of over £20,000 within a single day. As a result of my interpersonal skills, I was also elected as social secretary of the Union staff base, going on to organise various fundraising and social events. I believe that I can apply my interpersonal skills at Ashurst to forge strong relationships with my colleagues, fitting into the open and friendly culture of the firm. I also possess strong analytical skills that I apply to complete tasks with efficiency and purpose. For example, as a debt recovery paralegal, the firm took on a new client and received an influx of 1,000 cases spread between three team members. Over 100 of these cases were linked to the same debtor. This created confusion and inefficiency for the department as different team members were contacting and researching the same individual. Noticing these issues, I took the responsibility for the cases and considered how best to approach the task. The two issues I identified were (1) the lack of a single contact point to resolve the cases, and (2) the confusion caused by the spread of data across 100+ files. Firstly, I placed all the files in my name so that I could serve as the contact for the debtor going forwards. Secondly, I created a spreadsheet which contained the relevant information from all the linked accounts. Effectively, this collated the cases into a single document, which allowed all parties to easily input information to resolve the disputes. As a result of these actions, the files were closed within 6 weeks and we received a record-breaking payment of over £300,000. I believe I can apply these analytical skills to a career at Ashurst to approach tasks efficiently and effectively.

question_text: Describe what you think it takes to be a successful commercial lawyer and what are some of the challenges you might face as a trainee solicitor. (300 words)
sample_answer: The ability to communicate is an essential skill for any commercial lawyer. Whether it is with clients or colleagues, lawyers are frequently exchanging complex information and ideas. For a trainee, even receiving instruction from a supervisor requires clear communication; this lowers the risk of misunderstanding the task at hand and allows trainees to set realistic expectations. As a volunteer at Citizens Advice [redacted region of London], I would regularly hold difficult conversations with clients. One example is where I assisted a client who had difficulties speaking English. Despite language barriers, by using a calm and professional tone, I was able to guide the client through a Discretionary Housing Payment application over the phone. This resulted in a grant of over £3,000. I believe that I can apply my communication skills at Ashurst to communicate clearly with clients and colleagues. Adaptability is another crucial skill for a trainee to possess. Lawyers face a constantly changing field of work. Sudden deadlines can arrive seemingly from nowhere, and there are also wider technological and legislative developments. As such, it is crucial for lawyers to maintain flexibility in their work. Whilst working through my caseload as a debt recovery paralegal, my client requested that court proceedings be issued on over 50 cases with a strict deadline. As this task was specifically requested by the client, I reprioritised my work to focus on these cases. I also re-evaluated my previous duties, to ensure that any existing deadlines or court dates would not be missed. I was able to quickly adapt to the new 'CPC' online issuing system adopted by the firm to meet our client's request within 48 hours. I believe that I can apply my flexibility to be a successful trainee at Ashurst, adapting to shifting priorities that arise from newly issued urgent tasks.

question_text: Please tell us about a recent news article that interests you and how this relates to Ashurst? (300 words)
sample_answer: As outlined by the Financial Times, the proposed Nuclear Energy (Financing) (NE(F)) Bill is set to introduce the Regulated Asset Base (RAB) model to finance nuclear power station developments. This model will be used to fund Sizewell C, the first nuclear plant to be constructed in Britain since 1995. Nuclear projects are notoriously expensive and take decades to turn a profit; Sizewell C will cost over £10 billion in construction costs. The RAB model decreases risk for investors by charging a levy against consumer energy bills to subsidise developments. Hence, the NE(F) Bill will certainly promote private investment in nuclear projects. With the UK's most distinguished projects team - which has a heavy focus on clean energy - this measure could significantly impact Ashurst. The RAB model represents a new tool that Ashurst and its clients can use to finance potential nuclear projects. Ashurst does have experience in this area, having acted on the Thames Tideway Tunnel project which was funded in the same way. The measure may also introduce newcomers to the market, meaning that Ashurst could benefit from increased opportunities and investment within the energy industry. Taking a wider view, the NE(F) Bill is just one example of the rapidly increasing investment into the energy sector. The ongoing energy crisis has compounded Britain's goal to reach a net-zero economy by 2050. Labour leader, Keir Starmer recently announced his plans to launch Great British Energy - a publicly owned green energy provider - should he come into office, pledging £8 billion for investments into energy projects. This policy would represent further opportunity for Ashurst to advise on major energy developments. However, whilst it is lucrative, this also shows the energy industry is ever-changing. Therefore, Ashurst should maintain flexibility to ensure it can adapt to potential policy changes in the future.

question_text: Please explain your motivations for pursuing a career as a commercial solicitor and why you think Norton Rose Fulbright would be a good match for you (Maximum 750 words).
sample_answer: My interest in commercial law began during my time at Schroders, when my team was leading the compliance process with new European sustainability regulations. After reviewing a 200-page consultation paper, the directors in my team were still uncertain about the regulatory implications for our funds. The project progressed much quicker because the City lawyers advising us effectively explained the specific changes impacting our firm. I was so impressed by the lawyers' articulate nature and tailored advice that I explored the idea of becoming a solicitor myself. I confirmed this interest upon attending insight events at Paul Hastings, Baker McKenzie and Vinson & Elkins. When I was working on a case study on an international joint venture, I found myself supplementing my legal arguments with my understanding of Russian foreign policy and private equity investments. As someone with a wide range of academic interests, I really enjoyed how topical and multidisciplinary the analysis is in commercial law, especially compared to the heavily quantitative work in my former role. I believe law allows me to develop my existing interest in business and finance while capitalising on my natural strengths as a History and International Relations graduate. Above all, Norton Rose Fulbright's multicultural environment compelled me to apply. At the Energy Transition event, senior associate Melusi Dlamini shared that the firm's wide international reach allowed them to explore their interest in African energy work. As a Hongkonger that attended an international school with over 80 nationalities represented, I am eager to work with people from different regions. My roommates were from Bulgaria, Timor-Leste, and Mauritius respectively, and I learnt a lot from hearing their different perspectives on global issues. My knowledge of and passion for different cultures would be well-utilised and further developed at such a global firm. I am confident in my ability to build rapport with international clients, particularly in the international secondment. Secondly, I am drawn to Norton Rose Fulbright's unique industry focus, particularly its strengths in energy. From engaging with energy-related case studies and speaking with project financing lawyers at the Vinson & Elkins, I really enjoyed the tangibility of energy work. Partner Amy Armitage echoed this, where she said seeing the physical sites she worked on felt highly rewarding. The industry-focused structure means trainees can learn from lawyers with deep sectoral expertise and see projects throughout the whole lifecycle. Also, the firm's practice group has won not just accolades in their local markets, but also global Band 1 rankings for multi-jurisdictional work. This makes Norton Rose Fulbright the ideal place for me to explore potential areas I may specialise in upon qualification as a solicitor at an international law firm. I believe I have the key competencies to succeed as a commercial lawyer. Firstly, I am capable of dissecting complex information and making insightful observations. I produced a monthly firmwide update on the cross-border retail fund market, which the CEO often engaged with. From large datasets, I extract relevant data points to highlight top-selling sectors and funds, explaining trends and outliers with macroeconomic analysis. This required a high standard of analytical rigour, which is foundational to legal work. Secondly, I always take the initiative to learn and help others. My manager was on secondment and only worked Mondays and Fridays. I familiarised myself with the data and slides he regularly updates for the Sustainability ExCo in case queries come in mid-week. Later when there were urgent requests from the Chief Investment Officer, I was able to respond and support my manager and team. This shows that I am not afraid to challenge myself with greater responsibilities, and I proactively think of ways to support the team. I am also a self-starter that remains resilient in difficult circumstances. During my internship at BlackRock (made virtual during Covid), there was an 8-hour time difference as I was home in Hong Kong. Despite these setbacks, I was determined to maximise my learning as I lacked prior knowledge of finance compared to the economics students in my cohort. I used all means available to me, ranging from having coffee chats with 30 people across geographies and functions to self-studying the Bloomberg Market Concepts certification. I believe I have the grit to thrive in the high-stakes environment of a global law firm like Norton Rose Fulbright. (712 words)
